Where it began

Shaun Marsh was born in Narrogin, Western Australia, on 9 July 1983. Cricket ran in the family. His father, Geoff Marsh, played for Australia, and his younger brother Mitchell would go on to play for Australia too. His nickname, SOS, stands for Son of Swampy, a nod to his dad.

At Wesley College in Perth he and Mitchell both shone. In 1998 Shaun averaged 210 in the Darlot Cup, a schools record that lasted ten years. He played in two Under-19 World Cups for Australia, and the second, in 2002, ended with Australia lifting the trophy.

The player

He made his first-class debut for Western Australia in March 2001 and became a fixture in their side, later moving up to open like his father. In 2008 he won the Lawrie Sawle Medal as the state's best player, then topped the run charts in the first IPL for Kings XI Punjab.

His Test chance came in Sri Lanka in September 2011. His father presented him with his baggy green, and he made 141 in his first innings. Between 2011 and 2019 he played 38 Tests and scored 2,265 runs at 34.32, with six hundreds and a best of 182 against the West Indies at home.

What made him special

Marsh was a stylish left-hander who could bat anywhere in the top order. He also showed a knack for tricky conditions. In 2016 Australia's batsmen found Sri Lanka hard going and lost all three Tests, but when he was brought back for the last one he made 130.

His Test career came in stops and starts, and form did not always travel with him. Yet whenever Australia had a gap at the top of the order, the selectors seemed to find their way back to his name, which says plenty about how much they rated him.

Away from the middle

He was one of the best Twenty20 batsmen of his time. He won the orange cap for the most runs in the 2008 IPL, made the ESPNcricinfo IPL team in 2011, and finished the 2012–13 Big Bash as its leading scorer for Perth Scorchers. Later he played county cricket for Glamorgan, and in October 2020 he made his 30th first-class hundred. He retired from first-class cricket in March 2023.

And finally

Few families can match the Marshes for Australia caps around the dinner table. And few debutants have had a nicer start to a Test than Shaun, who was handed his baggy green by his own father.
